full_judgment:
2. The pre-emptor-respondents instituted the Miscellaneous Case No. 114 of 1968 under Section 96 of the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act claiming inter-alia, that plots Nos. 415 and 417 appertain to jama of Rs. 3-11-0 recorded in C.S. khatian No. 936, P.S. Narail, district Jessore belonging to Dabir Molla and others and plot No. 416 appertains to jama of Rs. 2-8-0 recorded in C.S. khatian No. 1580 of the same mouza and belonged to said Dabir Molla. Respondents became co-sharers by purchase of land from the said khatian on different dates from the different co-sharers. The appellant purchased .93 acres of land out of the 3 plots from the recorded tenants namely Abdul Hakim Molla and Matiar Rahman Molla, respondent Nos. 5 and 6. The respondents therefore, instituted the case for pre-eruption which, however, was resisted by the appellant-pre-emptor. 

 3. The trial Court allowed the pre-emption case. The appellate Court below, however, modified the judgment of the trial Court holding that the pre-emptors were co-sharers of the seller-respondent No. 6 only and the pre-emption of the land in plot No. 415 and 417 was refused holding that the land belonged to Abdul Hakim Molla which is recorded in a separate S.A. khatian, thereby disallowed the pre-emption in respect of .65 acres of land but allowed pre-emption of 17½ dec from the said khatian. The High Court Division considered the evidence on record and noticed that the kabala Exhibit B was pre-empted which shows 551 decimals of plot No. 415 recorded in C.S. khatian No. 936 was transferred to tilt O.P. No. 1. It was further noticed that Exhibit B is silent with regard to the alleged sub-tenancy of Abdul Hakim Molla and when the O. P. having purchased the sub-tenancy of Abdul Hakim Molla the story raised by him could not be accepted. In this view of the matter the Rule was made absolute and the order of the appellate Court below was set aside, and thejudgment and order passed by the learned Munsif was affirmed. 

 5. Exhibit B is the document under pre-emption. The deed itself did not show any separate tenancy and it was a C.S. khatian. The total land purchased from plot No. 415 and 417—.82½ acres of land. It was a C.S. khatian that was mentioned in the sale deed and that deed was pre-empted. No evidence is admissible to vary the contents of the documents by any oral evidence. The appellate Court below was clearly in error in not taking into view the provisions of Section 91 and 92 of the Evidence Act. The High Court Division correctly arrived at the finding that the sub tenancy is a myth and the explanation that on the wrong advice of the deed writer the document was drawn up is not tenable because in a pre-emption case it is the transfer which is sought to be pre-empted and the document of transfer in question is Exhibit B. The High Court Division had given cogent reasons for setting aside the findings of the appellate Court below. The respondents were co-sharers by purchase. This fact is not denied. The document sought to be pre-empted is the C.S. khatian and C.S. plots. The pre-emption case could not be refused on the ground that a sub-tenancy has been recorded in S.A. khatian. The trial Court noticed that the dakhilas Exhibit A series are spurious and concocted for the purpose of the case. The trial Court has given cogent reason for not accepting these dakhilas as genuine. For example the rent of 1352 and 1353 B.S. allegedly had been paid in 1361 B.S. when the claim was barred; again the rent of 1348 B.S. and 1349 B.S. was allegedly paid in 1359 B.S. and the Trial Court observed : "It is rather impossible that any tenant would pay his barred dues to his immediate landlord". It was noticed that education cess was shown for the year 1352 and 1353 B.S. although it was imposed from 1356 B.S. In view of these circumstances conclusion of the lower appellate Court that there was a separate tenancy of Abdul Hakim for the ka schedule land of Exhibit B does not hold good. The High Court Division rightly reversed the decision of the appellate Court below and allowed the pre-emption. In the result, therefore, this appeal is dismissed with cost.
